story.simple_summary: Team2 left a significant hole in the defensive block in their defensive half.
story.how_it_started: The whole defensive shape was too spread — this wasn't an isolated gap. The defensive line was sitting relatively deep. A player stepped forward or drifted wide without anyone covering the space left behind.
story.how_it_developed: It barely lasted a second, but in a dangerous position that's all it takes. The space sat close enough for a direct run at goal with no Team2 player in position to intercept a pass into it.
story.why_it_matters: That kind of gap gives an attacker time to receive, control and shoot. Opponents who read the game well will target this immediately.
story.coach_tip: Team2's defensive block needs to stay tighter as a unit. When one player moves, everyone adjusts — not just the nearest one.

story.simple_summary: One team2 attacker was completely free with no team1 player in range — right in front of goal — the most dangerous place to give anyone a free touch.
story.how_it_started: Team1 lost track of a runner during the phase of play. The run was timed to arrive behind the defensive line.
story.how_it_developed: Even that fraction of a second of freedom right in front of goal is enough for a quality player. One free attacker in this position is all it takes for a clear chance on goal.
story.why_it_matters: Allowing an attacker to receive freely right in front of goal is a direct route to a clear chance. There is no way to defend properly once the ball arrives at a free player in that area.
story.coach_tip: Each Team1 defender must own their runner — especially late runs from midfield. When the ball moves wide, always check what's happening in behind. Call it out loudly.

story.simple_summary: Team1 had 5 attackers against just 2 defenders — a clear overload with multiple free attackers right at the edge of the box.
story.how_it_started: Team1 runners moved forward and Team2 didn't track them. 5 attackers against just 2 defenders appeared right at the edge of the box.
story.how_it_developed: Even in that split second, a quality team will find the free man and shoot. Team2's remaining defender had no realistic chance of covering all the threats.
story.why_it_matters: Numerical overloads in front of goal are one of the clearest routes to a shot on target. When a defence is outnumbered that close to goal, errors are almost guaranteed.
story.coach_tip: A midfielder needs to track the runners earlier. By the time Team2 realised they were outnumbered, it was too late to recover. The solution is tracking movement before the ball arrives — not reacting to it after.

story.why_it_matters: A gap that wide is virtually indefensible without a recovery run. Opponents who read the game well will target this immediately.
story.coach_tip: Team2's defensive block needs to stay tighter as a unit. When one player moves, everyone adjusts — not just the nearest one.

story.simple_summary: Team2's defensive block was too spread to be effective as a defensive unit.
story.how_it_started: Players gradually moved out of their defensive positions. Around the middle of the pitch — gaps here allow balls in behind.
story.how_it_developed: The disorganisation held for a few seconds — enough time for a threatening ball in. With the block this open, passing lanes appeared between and behind Team2's lines.
story.why_it_matters: When the block is that open, any ball into the space between lines is almost impossible to defend.
story.coach_tip: When Team2 defends, the spacing between players should stay tight. Every time someone moves, the player next to them must adjust. It's a collective responsibility — one player drifting breaks the whole unit.

story.simple_summary: Team1 had 4 attackers against just 1 defender — a clear overload with multiple free attackers right at the edge of the box.
story.how_it_started: Team1 runners moved forward and Team2 didn't track them. 4 attackers against just 1 defender appeared right at the edge of the box.
story.how_it_developed: Even in that split second, a quality team will find the free man and shoot. Team2's remaining defender had no realistic chance of covering all the threats.
story.why_it_matters: Numerical overloads in front of goal are one of the clearest routes to a shot on target. When a defence is outnumbered that close to goal, errors are almost guaranteed.
story.coach_tip: A midfielder needs to track the runners earlier. By the time Team2 realised they were outnumbered, it was too late to recover. The solution is tracking movement before the ball arrives — not reacting to it after.

story.simple_summary: One team2 attacker was completely free with no team1 player in range — right in front of goal — the most dangerous place to give anyone a free touch.
story.how_it_started: Team1 lost track of a runner during the phase of play. The run was timed to arrive behind the defensive line.
story.how_it_developed: Even that fraction of a second of freedom right in front of goal is enough for a quality player. One free attacker in this position is all it takes for a clear chance on goal.
story.why_it_matters: Allowing an attacker to receive freely right in front of goal is a direct route to a clear chance. There is no way to defend properly once the ball arrives at a free player in that area.
story.coach_tip: Each Team1 defender must own their runner — especially late runs from midfield. When the ball moves wide, always check what's happening in behind. Call it out loudly.
